title: Capacity Planning for One Service
objectives: Turn daily users and per-user actions into peak read and write rates
Estimate storage growth and the RAM needed for a hot set
Decide which number drives the design: reads, writes, storage or memory

cards.title: Four numbers decide most designs
cards.body: Before choosing a database or a cache, estimate four things for the service: peak reads per second, peak writes per second, how fast stored data grows, and how much of it is hot enough to keep in memory. Each one points at a different bottleneck, and the largest one shapes the design.

cards.title: Worked example: a feed service at 10M daily users
cards.body: Each user reads 40 items and posts 2 a day, 1 KB per post. Reads: 10M × 40 = 400M a day, about 4,600 per second on average and about 14K at a 3x peak. Writes: 10M × 2 = 20M a day, about 230 per second and about 700 at peak. Storage grows 20 GB a day, about 7.3 TB a year. If the last 7 days are hot, that is 140 GB of hot data.

cards.title: From users to resources
cards.body: Every estimate is a chain of multiplications with stated assumptions.
steps: Daily active users × actions per user = actions per day
Actions per day ÷ 86,400 = average per second; × peak factor = peak
Writes per day × bytes per write = storage growth per day
Growth per day × hot days = memory for the hot set
Compare each result with what one node can handle

cards.title: The read:write ratio picks the tools
cards.body: A 20:1 read-heavy service benefits from caches and read replicas. A write-heavy service, such as event ingestion, needs cheap appends, partitioning and batching instead; a cache does little for data that is written once and rarely read again.

cards.title: Trap: sizing memory for all the data
cards.body: Holding every byte ever written in RAM is rarely needed. Most requests touch recent or popular data. Size the cache for the hot set, measure the hit rate, and let older data live on disk.

questions.prompt: A service gets 50 reads for every write. Which change usually helps its peak load the most?

choices.label: A cache in front of the reads
Faster disks for the write path
Larger write batches from clients
More partitions for the write log

questions.explanation: With reads dominating, serving them from memory removes most of the load.

questions.prompt: Why multiply the daily average by a peak factor?

choices.label: Daily averages already include the busiest hour
Traffic bunches into busy hours, and capacity must cover them
It converts the daily request count into bytes needed for storage
It accounts for the size of each response

questions.explanation: Users are not spread evenly over 24 hours; the evening peak can be several times the average.

questions.prompt: A service stores 7 TB but 90% of reads hit posts from the last week (140 GB). What should the cache be sized for?

choices.label: All 7 TB, so no read misses
The 140 GB hot set, then measure the hit rate
A fixed 1 GB, since caches should stay very small
Half of the total data, as a safe middle

questions.explanation: Size for the working set; the long tail of old data can stay on disk.

questions.prompt: An ingestion service writes 50K events per second and they are read once, by a nightly job. What matters most?

choices.label: A large read cache in front of the event store
Read replicas in more regions for the nightly job
Cheap appends, batching and partitioned storage
Keeping all events in RAM until the job runs

questions.explanation: Write-once, read-rarely data is limited by write throughput and storage, not reads.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of a capacity estimate.

items.label: Apply a peak factor
Compare with per-node limits
State users and actions per user
Compute storage growth and the hot set
Compute daily volume, then per second

questions.explanation: Inputs, volume, peak, data size, then the comparison that decides the design.

questions.prompt: A feed has 10M people reading 40 posts apiece each day. Spread across the day, how many reads per second is that?
questions.explanation: Sanity check: at a 3x peak that is about 14K reads/s, a load a cache handles easily but a single database would feel.

flashcards.back: Peak reads/s, peak writes/s, storage growth, hot-set memory.
Divide by 86,400 (about 10^5), then apply a peak factor.
The recent or popular data most requests touch; size caches for it, not for all data.

sources.title: Google SRE book: Introduction (Demand Forecasting and Capacity Planning)

mechanism.title: How a capacity estimate is built
steps: Start from stated inputs: daily active users, actions per user per day split into reads and writes, the size of each stored item, and how long data is kept. Write them down, because every later number inherits their error, and an interviewer or reviewer can only check what is stated.

Convert daily volume to a rate. A day has 86,400 seconds, about 10^5, so 400M reads a day is about 4,600 per second on average. Traffic is uneven, so multiply by a peak factor taken from real traffic graphs; 2 to 5 times the average is common for consumer services with an evening peak.

Storage growth is writes per day times bytes per write, plus overhead for indexes and replicas. 20M writes of 1 KB is 20 GB a day before replication; with three replicas the disk footprint is 60 GB a day. Over a year that adds up to tens of terabytes, which decides whether one machine or a partitioned store is needed.

Memory follows the access pattern, not the total size. If most reads hit the last week of data, the hot set is a week of writes. Caching it gives a high hit rate; caching more gives diminishing returns. Measure the hit rate after launch and adjust, because popularity curves differ by product.

Finally compare each number with what one node can do, using measured benchmarks for the chosen software and hardware. The largest ratio between demand and single-node capacity is the bottleneck, and the design should address that one first: caching for reads, partitioning for writes or storage, more memory for the hot set.

useWhen: Choosing between a single database and a partitioned store.
Sizing caches, replicas and disks before a launch.
avoidWhen: Avoid precise-looking numbers from guessed inputs; keep one or two significant figures.
Avoid planning from averages alone; size for the peak.

numbers.title: The feed service in numbers
assumptions: 10M daily users, 40 reads and 2 writes each per day
1 KB per post, 3x peak, the last 7 days are hot
steps: Reads: 10M × 40 = 400M a day; 400M ÷ 86,400 ≈ 4,630 per second; about 14K at peak.
Writes: 10M × 2 = 20M a day; about 230 per second; about 700 at peak.
Storage: 20M writes of 1 KB each is 20 GB a day; about 7.3 TB a year before replication.
Hot set: 20 GB × 7 = 140 GB, about three cache nodes with 48 GB usable each.
numbers.result: Reads dominate and the hot set fits a small cache cluster, so the first design move is a cache in front of a modest database.

india.title: How capacity planning is described
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The Google SRE book’s introduction treats demand forecasting and capacity planning as a core SRE responsibility. It lists the steps it considers mandatory: an organic demand forecast that extends beyond the lead time for acquiring capacity, inorganic demand such as launches and marketing pushes, and regular load testing to map raw resources, such as servers and disks, to service capacity. The Redis documentation on key eviction describes LRU and LFU policies that keep the most used keys when memory is full.

pitfalls.trap: “We have 10 TB, so we need 10 TB of cache.”
pitfalls.say: “I’d size the cache for the hot set, about a week of writes here, and check the hit rate.”

pitfalls.trap: “Average QPS is 4,600, so one server is fine.”
pitfalls.say: “The peak is about three times that, and I’d keep headroom for losing a node.”

takeaways: Estimate peak reads, peak writes, storage growth and the hot set.
Divide daily volume by 86,400 and apply a peak factor.
The read:write ratio decides between caching and write scaling; check which resource needs the most machines.
Size memory for the hot set, not for all the data.

interactive.title: Size the feed service
interactive.prompt: Each user reads 40 items and posts 2 a day at 1 KB; the peak is 3x and the last 7 days are hot. Assume one database node serves 10K reads/s or 5K writes/s and holds 10 TB, and one cache node holds 48 GB (illustrative). Slide daily active users and see which resource needs the most machines.
interactive.takeaway: At 10M users, uncached reads would need 2 database nodes while writes and a year of data fit on one; a 3-node cache holding the 140 GB hot set takes the reads off the database. Writes and storage only become the bottleneck at much larger sizes.

seeAlso.why: The general estimation habits behind these numbers
Where a cache sits once reads dominate

title: Storage Engines: B-trees vs LSM-trees
objectives: Explain how a B-tree updates pages in place and an LSM-tree appends and compacts
Compare write, read and space amplification
Pick an engine for a write-heavy or a read-heavy workload

cards.title: Two ways to keep data sorted on disk
cards.body: A B-tree keeps sorted data in fixed-size pages and changes a page where it lives. An LSM-tree (log-structured merge-tree) buffers writes in memory, flushes them as new sorted files, and merges those files in the background. Both answer the same queries; they pay for them at different times.

cards.title: Worked example: one small update
cards.body: Changing a 100-byte row in a B-tree-organised table (a clustered index) rewrites the 8 KB page that holds it, plus a log record: about 8,192 ÷ 100 ≈ 82 bytes written per byte changed, before counting index pages. An LSM-tree appends the new row to its log and memory table at once, but compaction may rewrite it several more times as files are merged level by level.

cards.title: The LSM write path
cards.body: Writes are sequential; the cost moves to background merging and to reads.
steps: Append the write to a log for durability
Insert it into a sorted in-memory table
Flush the full table to disk as an immutable sorted file
Compaction merges files and drops overwritten or deleted rows
Reads check memory, then files from newest to oldest, skipping files by filter

cards.title: Three kinds of amplification
cards.body: Write amplification is bytes written to disk per byte the application wrote. Read amplification is how many places a lookup must check. Space amplification is disk used per byte of live data. B-trees usually read less and write more per update; LSM-trees write in large sequential batches, but a read may consult several files and old versions take space until compaction.

cards.title: Trap: “LSM is always faster for writes”
cards.body: LSM ingestion is cheap at first, but compaction must keep up. If writes outpace merging, files pile up, reads slow down and the engine eventually throttles writers. Measure sustained throughput, not the first minutes of a benchmark.

questions.prompt: What does a B-tree do when one row in a page changes?

choices.label: Appends the row to a new sorted file and merges it in later compaction
Rewrites the page that holds the row, after logging the change
Stores only the changed bytes and nothing else
Rebuilds the whole index from the table

questions.explanation: B-trees update pages in place; the write-ahead log makes that safe.

questions.prompt: Why can an LSM-tree read touch several files?

choices.label: A key may exist in memory and in several sorted files
Each sorted file stores a single column of the table rows
Files are stored out of key order
The engine keeps two copies of each row on disk

questions.explanation: Newer versions sit in newer files; a lookup checks newest first and filters skip files without the key.

questions.prompt: An engine writes 30 GB to disk while the application writes 1 GB. What is that?

choices.label: Read amplification of 30
Space amplification of 30
Write amplification of 30
A replication factor of 30

questions.explanation: Bytes written to disk per byte written by the application.

questions.prompt: A time-series service ingests many small writes and mostly reads recent ranges. Which engine fits well?

choices.label: An LSM-tree, for cheap sequential ingestion
A B-tree, since reads are mostly range scans
Either one, as engines barely differ on write cost
A hash index, for constant-time point writes

questions.explanation: High-volume small appends suit LSM-trees, which still serve recent ranges from sorted files; hash indexes cannot serve range scans.

questions.prompt: Order the life of a write in an LSM-tree.

items.label: Flush the table to a sorted file
Append to the log
Merge files during compaction
Insert into the memory table

questions.explanation: Durable first, then in memory, then on disk, then merged.

questions.prompt: A 100-byte row changes in an 8 KB (8,192-byte) page that is written back whole. Roughly what is the write amplification?
assumptions: Only the data page is counted, not the log or index pages
questions.explanation: Sanity check: small random updates are where B-trees pay most; the log and index pages add more on top.

flashcards.back: Rewrite the page in place, after logging the change.
Log, memory table, flush to sorted file, merge later by compaction.
Write: disk bytes per app byte. Read: places checked. Space: disk per live byte.

mechanism.title: How the two engines spend their I/O
steps: A B-tree stores rows or keys in fixed-size pages, often 8 KB or 16 KB, arranged as a shallow tree. A lookup reads one page per level, usually three or four, and the top levels stay in memory. An update finds the page, changes it in memory, logs the change, and later writes the whole page back. PostgreSQL differs for tables: they are heap files and an update writes a new row version (MVCC) rather than changing the old one, and full-page images in the WAL after each checkpoint add further write amplification.

Writing whole pages for small changes is the B-tree’s write amplification. Random updates across a large table touch different pages, so the disk sees scattered page writes. In exchange, a read finds the single current version of a row in one place.

An LSM-tree turns writes into sequential appends. Each write goes to a log and an in-memory sorted table. When the table fills, it is flushed as an immutable sorted file. Deletes are written as markers called tombstones, because files are never edited in place.

Compaction merges files to discard overwritten rows and tombstones and to bound how many files a read must check. Levelled compaction keeps files in levels of growing size and rewrites data each time it moves down a level, trading extra writes for fewer files per read. Other strategies merge less often, writing less but leaving more files and more space used.

Reads in an LSM-tree check the memory table and then files from newest to oldest. Per-file filters, such as Bloom filters, answer “definitely not here” for most files, so a point lookup usually reads one or two. Range scans must merge sorted runs from several files, which costs more than a B-tree range scan.

useWhen: LSM-trees for write-heavy ingestion such as logs, metrics and events.
B-trees for read-heavy, update-in-place workloads with many range queries.
avoidWhen: Avoid judging an LSM engine on a short benchmark before compaction starts.
Avoid B-trees for huge append-only streams where random page writes dominate.

numbers.title: Small updates in an 8 KB page
assumptions: 1,000 updates per second spread over a large table
steps: Each update dirties one page: 8,192 ÷ 100 ≈ 82 bytes written per byte changed.
At 1,000 updates per second that is up to 1,000 × 8 KB ≈ 8 MB/s of page writes, before the log.
If many updates hit the same hot pages between writes to disk, they share one page write, so the real figure is often lower.
An LSM-tree writes the same 100 KB/s sequentially, then rewrites it during compaction a number of times that depends on its levels.
numbers.result: Neither engine avoids amplification; they choose where to pay it. Measure with the real access pattern.

india.title: What the documentation says
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The PostgreSQL documentation describes tables and indexes stored as arrays of fixed-size pages, normally 8 kB, with each page holding row pointers and tuples; an update writes a new tuple version rather than overwriting the old one. Apache Cassandra’s documentation describes writes going to a commit log and an in-memory structure, flushed to immutable sorted files, with compaction strategies that trade write amplification against the number of files a read must touch.

pitfalls.say: “They make writes sequential; I’d check compaction can keep up and what range reads cost.”

pitfalls.trap: “A B-tree update writes only the changed row.”
pitfalls.say: “It rewrites the page, so small random updates have high write amplification.”

takeaways: B-trees update pages in place; LSM-trees append and compact.
Every engine pays write, read or space amplification somewhere.
Compaction must keep pace with ingestion.
Choose by workload: write-heavy streams vs read-heavy updates and ranges.

interactive.title: Which engine for the metrics store?
interactive.prompt: A service ingests 200K small metric points per second and dashboards read the last hour by time range. Which storage engine suits it better, and why?

choices.label: An LSM-tree: sequential appends absorb the write rate
choices.feedback: Right: ingestion dominates, and recent data stays in few, recent files.

choices.label: A B-tree: one page per lookup keeps the reads fast
choices.feedback: Reads are cheap either way here; scattered page rewrites at 200K writes/s are the real risk.

choices.label: A hash index: constant-time writes and reads
choices.feedback: Hash indexes cannot serve the time-range reads the dashboards need.

interactive.reveal: With a write rate this high, turning writes into sequential appends matters most. The cost moves to compaction, so plan disk bandwidth for it and keep an eye on the number of files per read.

seeAlso.why: B-tree and LSM indexes in system design terms
How B-tree and hash indexes serve lookups

title: Preventing Double Booking
objectives: Spot the check-then-insert race behind double bookings
Compare constraints, row locks, optimistic versions and serializable isolation
Choose a fix that holds under concurrent requests

cards.title: The race in check-then-insert
cards.body: A booking handler reads “is seat 12A free?”, sees yes, and inserts a booking. Two requests can both read “free” before either inserts, and both succeed. Each request is correct on its own; together they break the rule that a seat has one booking.

cards.title: Worked example: two requests, 5 ms apart
cards.body: At 10:00:00.000 request A checks seat 12A and finds it free. At 10:00:00.005 request B checks and also finds it free, because A has not committed yet. A inserts and commits at .010, B at .015. Under the default read-committed isolation in many databases, nothing stops B; the flight now has two passengers in 12A.

cards.title: Five ways to make the check stick
cards.body: Each one makes the second request fail or wait instead of double booking.
steps: Unique constraint on (flight, seat): the second insert fails
Keep one row per seat and lock it first: the second request waits, then sees it taken
Conditional update: book the seat only where it is still free; zero rows means it is gone
Serializable isolation: the database aborts one transaction
Turn the failure into a clear “seat just taken” reply

cards.title: Lock, conditional update or optimistic
cards.body: A row lock (pessimistic) makes contenders wait. A single conditional update holds no lock across user think time and needs no retry: the loser learns the seat is gone. Optimistic concurrency reads a version and retries on a mismatch; it suits rare conflicts, not hot seats.

cards.title: Trap: checking in the application only
cards.body: A check in application code, even inside a transaction, does not stop a concurrent insert under read committed or snapshot isolation. The guarantee must come from the database: a constraint, a lock, a conditional update, or serializable isolation.

questions.prompt: Two requests both read “seat free” and both insert. What is this?

choices.label: A deadlock between the two transactions
A check-then-act race
A dirty read of uncommitted data
A lost connection during commit

questions.explanation: The decision was based on a read that another transaction made stale.

questions.prompt: Which fix makes the second insert fail even if the code forgets to check?

choices.label: Logging every booking attempt
A cache of the free seats kept in app memory
Retrying the insert on timeout
A unique constraint on flight and seat

questions.explanation: Constraints are enforced by the database for every writer.

questions.prompt: Under snapshot isolation, two transactions insert different rows after each checked the same rule. What can happen?

choices.label: Both commit and the rule is broken
The second always waits for the first
Both are aborted by the database
The second reads the first one’s insert

questions.explanation: This is write skew: no row was written twice, so snapshot isolation sees no conflict.

questions.prompt: Concert tickets: thousands of buyers hit the same few seats in seconds. Which approach fits best?

choices.label: Optimistic versions, since conflicts are rare
A read-only replica for the seat check
Locking or a conditional update on the seat row
Checking seat availability twice in the booking code

questions.explanation: With frequent conflicts, optimistic retries waste work; a lock or atomic conditional update settles each seat once.

questions.prompt: Order a pessimistic booking transaction.

items.label: Check that it is free
Begin the transaction
Mark the seat booked and commit
Lock the seat’s own row

questions.explanation: Lock the seat row before the check, so the check stays true until commit.

questions.prompt: A hotel has 50 rooms and 49 are booked. Three requests check at the same moment, all see a free room, and all insert with no constraint. How many bookings exist afterwards?
questions.explanation: Sanity check: the overbooking equals the number of racing requests minus the rooms that were really free.

flashcards.back: Two requests can read “free” before either commits.
Two transactions read the same rule, write different rows, and both commit.
Unique constraint, row lock, version check, serializable isolation.

mechanism.title: Why the read does not protect the write
steps: Most databases default to read committed or snapshot isolation. A transaction sees committed data, but nothing it reads is locked against other writers. When the decision to insert depends on a read, another transaction can change what that read would return before the insert commits.

If both transactions update the same row, the database notices: one waits or fails. Double booking is harder because the two transactions insert different rows. Snapshot isolation, used for repeatable read in several databases, allows this write skew.

A unique constraint turns the business rule into something the database enforces on every insert: only one row per flight and seat. The second insert fails with a constraint error, which the handler turns into “seat just taken”. For overlapping ranges, such as hotel nights, some databases offer exclusion constraints; otherwise model each night as a row.

Keep one row per seat or room-night so there is something to lock or update. A row lock, taken by reading that row “for update” before checking, makes the second transaction wait until the first commits, then re-check. A conditional update is a separate, lock-free option: one statement sets the seat to booked only where it is still free, and zero rows updated means the seat is gone, with no retry loop. Optimistic concurrency, in contrast, reads a version, writes only if it is unchanged and retries on a mismatch; it suits edits that rarely collide.

Serializable isolation detects that the two transactions could not have run one after the other and aborts one of them. It protects every rule without changing the schema, but the application must retry aborted transactions, and heavy contention increases aborts.

useWhen: Bookings, inventory, unique usernames and any “at most N” rule.
Flows where a read decides whether a write is allowed.
avoidWhen: Avoid relying on an application-level check alone.
Avoid holding locks while waiting for a user or a remote call.

rows: Needs a rule that fits a key
Rule must fit one row’s state

numbers.title: How many bookings slip through
assumptions: 3 requests check at the same moment
steps: All 3 see one free room.
All 3 insert: 49 + 3 = 52 bookings.
With a unique constraint per room and night, 1 insert succeeds and 2 fail.
With a row lock, the 2 later requests wait, re-check and see no free room.
numbers.result: The overbooking equals the racing requests minus the free rooms; any of the four fixes brings it to zero.

india.title: What the PostgreSQL documentation says
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The PostgreSQL documentation on transaction isolation explains that read committed lets each statement see data committed before it began, and that repeatable read in PostgreSQL uses a snapshot. It describes serialization anomalies (write skew is one kind) and states that the serializable level detects them and aborts a transaction, which the application must be prepared to retry.

pitfalls.trap: “We check availability inside a transaction, so it is safe.”
pitfalls.say: “The read is not locked; I’d add a unique constraint or lock the row.”
“For a few hot seats with many buyers, I’d lock or use an atomic conditional update.”

takeaways: Check-then-insert races under default isolation.
Make the database enforce the rule: constraint, lock, conditional update or serializable.
Lock for hot items; use versions when conflicts are rare.
Turn the conflict into a clear reply and retry where it makes sense.

interactive.title: Stop the double booking
interactive.prompt: A cinema app checks “seat free?” then inserts a booking. During a premiere, 2,000 people click the same 20 seats in the first second. Which change prevents double bookings and handles the rush best?

choices.label: Retry the insert if it times out
choices.feedback: Retries do nothing about two requests that both saw the seat as free.

choices.label: Atomic conditional update: book the seat only where it is still free
choices.feedback: Right: each seat is taken once, and every loser learns at once that it is gone.

choices.label: Optimistic versions with automatic retry until success
choices.feedback: It prevents duplicates, but each retry re-reads and loses again, adding a round of reads and writes per buyer; a single conditional update settles it in one statement.

interactive.reveal: The fix must live in the database. Under heavy contention, an atomic conditional update or a short row lock settles each seat once; a unique constraint is the safety net that catches any code path that forgets.

seeAlso.why: The isolation anomalies behind write skew

title: Operating a Dead-Letter Queue
objectives: Decide which failures skip retries and go straight to the dead-letter queue
Keep enough context and retention to fix and replay parked messages
Alert on, inspect and redrive a dead-letter queue safely

cards.title: Recap, then the hard part
cards.body: Message Queues and Background Jobs introduced poison messages and dead-letter queues. This lesson is about running one: what goes there, what to keep with it, who is alerted, and how to replay safely.

cards.title: Worked example: five tries, then park it
cards.body: A consumer retries a failing message with backoff of 1, 2, 4 and 8 seconds between five attempts, a total wait of 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 = 15 seconds. After the fifth failure it moves the message to a dead-letter queue and carries on with the next one. An alert fires, an engineer finds a missing field, fixes the producer, and replays the parked message.

cards.title: Where failing messages go
cards.body: Transient failures are retried; persistent ones are parked, not dropped.
steps: Consumer receives the message and tries to process it
On failure, retry with backoff while the attempt count is under the limit
At the limit, move the message to the dead-letter queue with the error
Alert on dead-letter queue depth
After a fix, redrive the messages back to the main queue

cards.title: Keep enough to act on
cards.body: Park each message with its error, attempt count, consumer version and first-failure time. Set the queue’s retention longer than your worst time to fix, or parked messages expire before anyone replays them.

cards.title: Trap: a dead-letter queue nobody watches
cards.body: Parking messages hides the failure from the main flow. Without an alert on its depth and a way to replay, the dead-letter queue becomes a place where orders and payments silently disappear. Treat a growing dead-letter queue as an incident.

questions.prompt: A message fails with “missing field: customer_id” on every attempt. What is it?

choices.label: A transient failure that more retries will clear
A poison message that will never succeed as is
A duplicate that the consumer already handled
A message that arrived out of order

questions.explanation: The failure is in the content, so retrying cannot change the outcome.

questions.prompt: Why cap the number of delivery attempts?

choices.label: So one failing message cannot block the queue or burn capacity
Because brokers delete any message after three failed deliveries
To turn at-least-once delivery into exactly-once
To keep the consumer’s memory use constant

questions.explanation: Unbounded retries turn one bad message into an outage for everything behind it.

questions.prompt: Which failure should skip retries and go straight to the dead-letter queue?

choices.label: A timeout calling the payments service
A message that fails schema validation
A database deadlock that aborted the transaction
A 503 from a dependency that is shedding load

questions.explanation: Invalid content fails the same way every time; the others are transient and worth a few spaced retries.

questions.prompt: After a producer bug is fixed, 3,000 orders sit in the dead-letter queue. What is the safe next step?

choices.label: Delete them, since they are old
Redrive them to the main queue with idempotent consumers
Apply them by hand with SQL updates in the orders database
Leave them as a record of the incident

questions.explanation: Replaying through the normal path is safe when consumers ignore duplicates.

questions.prompt: Order the handling of a message that keeps failing.

items.label: Move it to the dead-letter queue with the error
Fix the cause and redrive
Retry with backoff up to the limit
Alert on the dead-letter queue depth

questions.explanation: Bound the retries, park it, make it visible, then replay after the fix.

questions.prompt: A consumer waits 1, 2, 4 and 8 seconds between five attempts. How many seconds pass between the first attempt and the move to the dead-letter queue, ignoring processing time?
questions.explanation: Sanity check: the backoff should be long enough to outlast a short outage of a dependency, or transient failures land in the dead-letter queue too.

flashcards.back: A message that fails on every attempt because of its content.
Where messages go after the retry limit, with the error, for inspection and replay.
Fix the cause, replay through the normal path, keep consumers idempotent.

mechanism.title: How retries, limits and dead-letter queues fit together
steps: Message brokers deliver at least once. If a consumer fails or crashes before acknowledging, the broker delivers the message again. That is what makes queues reliable for transient failures, and it is also why a message that can never succeed keeps coming back.

In a strictly ordered stream, such as a partition consumed in order, the consumer cannot skip a message without giving up ordering. A poison message at the head stops the partition. In an unordered queue, it is redelivered among the others and keeps using consumer time on every attempt.

A retry limit counts deliveries per message. Many brokers track a receive count and move the message to a configured dead-letter queue when it passes the maximum. Consumers can also classify errors: validation failures go straight to the dead-letter queue, while timeouts get retries with exponential backoff and jitter.

The dead-letter queue keeps the original message and, ideally, the error, the attempt count and the consumer version. Operators alert on its depth or age, inspect a sample, fix the producer or the consumer, and then redrive: move the messages back to the source queue to be processed normally.

Redrive delivers messages again, possibly long after they were first sent. Consumers must be idempotent, and handlers should check that the action still makes sense, for example that an order has not been cancelled since. For ordered streams, a parked message can leave later messages for the same entity applied before it, so some systems park the whole entity’s messages together.

useWhen: Any queue or stream consumer whose input can be malformed or refer to missing data.
Pipelines where losing a message is worse than delaying it.
avoidWhen: Avoid infinite redelivery with no limit.
Avoid a dead-letter queue with no alert, owner or replay path.

rows: Short outages fill the dead-letter queue
A poison message blocks or burns capacity longer
Misclassified errors are parked or retried wrongly

numbers.title: How long a message takes to reach the dead-letter queue
steps: Waits between attempts: 1, 2, 4 and 8 s.
Total: 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 = 15 s from first attempt to parking.
A dependency outage of 10 s is ridden out; one of 60 s is not.
Adding jitter spreads the retries of many messages so they do not arrive together.
numbers.result: The retry schedule decides which outages are absorbed; anything longer belongs in the dead-letter queue, with an alert.

india.title: How managed queues describe it
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The Amazon SQS developer guide describes a redrive policy that moves a message to a dead-letter queue after it has been received a configured maximum number of times, and a redrive feature to move messages back after the cause is fixed. Google Cloud Pub/Sub documents dead-letter topics that receive messages after a maximum number of delivery attempts.

pitfalls.say: “I’d cap attempts, park failures with the error, and alert on the dead-letter queue.”

pitfalls.trap: “Messages in the dead-letter queue are lost anyway.”
pitfalls.say: “They are parked for replay; after the fix I’d redrive them through idempotent consumers.”

takeaways: At-least-once delivery redelivers failures, including poison messages.
Bound retries with backoff; park the rest in a dead-letter queue.
Alert on dead-letter depth and own the replay.
Redrive only into idempotent consumers.

interactive.title: The stuck partition
interactive.prompt: An ordered consumer of a payments stream hits a message whose amount field is text, not a number. It retries forever. What happens to the other payments in that partition?

choices.label: They wait behind it until the message is removed
choices.feedback: Right: in-order consumption cannot pass the head, so the whole partition stalls.

choices.label: The broker skips the bad message after a while
choices.feedback: Nothing skips it: the consumer keeps re-reading it until a retry limit or the consumer moves it aside.

choices.label: Other consumers pick them up in parallel
choices.feedback: A partition is consumed in order by one consumer at a time in a group; others do not jump ahead.

interactive.reveal: Bound the attempts and move the message to a dead-letter queue with its error, then alert. Because this is a payments stream, decide whether later payments for the same account should wait with it to keep their order.

seeAlso.why: Background jobs and how workers retry them

title: Clocks, Time and Ordering in Services
objectives: Tell wall-clock time from monotonic time and use each correctly
Explain how clock skew breaks last-write-wins and ordering by timestamp
Order events with versions or sequence numbers instead

cards.title: Two clocks on every machine
cards.body: A wall clock tells the date and time and can be adjusted: time synchronisation may step it forward or back. A monotonic clock only ever moves forward and is meant for measuring durations. Use the monotonic clock for timeouts and latency, and wall time only to record when something happened.

cards.title: Worked example: a 300 ms skew loses a write
cards.body: Server A’s clock runs 300 ms fast. A user saves a profile through A at a true time of 10:00:00.000, stamped 10:00:00.300. They save again 200 ms later through B, stamped 10:00:00.200. Last-write-wins keeps the larger timestamp, so the older save from A wins and the newer one is silently lost.

cards.title: Ordering without trusting clocks
cards.body: Give the order a single source or carry it in the data.
steps: Let one writer per item assign increasing version numbers
Or let the database assign a sequence at commit
Send the version with each update; reject stale ones
Use logical clocks when many writers must agree on causality
Keep wall time for display and logs only

cards.title: Skew is normal, not an error
cards.body: Synchronised clocks on servers in one data centre often agree within a few milliseconds, but drift, pauses and misconfiguration can push skew much higher, and phones can be off by minutes. Any design that compares timestamps from different machines must state how much skew it tolerates.

cards.title: Trap: measuring a timeout with wall time
cards.body: If a timeout is computed as “now minus start” with the wall clock and the clock steps back 2 seconds, the elapsed time can go negative and the timeout fires late by the size of the step; a step forward fires it early. Durations belong to the monotonic clock.

questions.prompt: Which clock should measure how long a request took?

choices.label: The wall clock, since it shows the real time
The client’s clock, sent in the request
The database server’s wall clock
The monotonic clock, which never steps back

questions.explanation: Durations need a clock that cannot jump when time is corrected.

questions.prompt: A service records latency as wall-clock end minus start. Mid-request, time sync steps the clock back 2 s. What does that sample show?

choices.label: A latency about 2 s too low, maybe negative
The true latency, as steps are rare
A latency about 2 s too high
No value, as the system drops that one sample

questions.explanation: The end time moved back 2 s, so the difference shrinks by 2 s; a monotonic clock avoids this.

questions.prompt: How can a service apply updates to one document in the right order?

choices.label: Sort updates by the client device’s timestamp
Use a version number assigned by one writer or the database
Apply whichever update arrives last over the network
Round each timestamp to the nearest second so skew is hidden

questions.explanation: A single source of versions gives an order that does not depend on clocks.

questions.prompt: A lease holder thinks its 10 s lease has 1 s left; the lock service’s clock says it expired. What is the safe design?

choices.label: Trust the holder, since it took the lease
Extend each lease to 60 s so it cannot expire mid-write
Use a fencing token the storage checks on every write
Synchronise clocks before each write

questions.explanation: Fencing tokens let the storage reject writes from a holder whose lease has passed, whatever its clock says.

questions.prompt: Order a versioned update that cannot apply out of order.

items.label: On a mismatch, re-read and retry or report
Change it locally
Read the document and its version
Write only if the version is unchanged

questions.explanation: The version, not a timestamp, decides whether the write is still based on the latest state.

questions.prompt: Server A’s clock is 300 ms fast and server B’s is 100 ms slow. With last-write-wins on timestamps, for how many milliseconds after a write on A can a real later write on B still lose?
assumptions: A is 300 ms ahead of true time, B is 100 ms behind
questions.workedAnswer: 300 + 100 = 400 ms of skew between A and B
questions.explanation: Sanity check: the window is the skew between the two clocks, not either clock’s error alone.

flashcards.back: Wall: date and time, can step. Monotonic: only forward, for durations.
With skew, an older write can carry a larger timestamp.
Versions from one writer or the database, or logical clocks.

mechanism.title: Why timestamps from different machines do not order events
steps: Every machine keeps time with a local oscillator that drifts. Time synchronisation, such as NTP, measures the offset to reference servers and corrects it, either by slewing the clock gradually or by stepping it when the offset is large. Between corrections, clocks on different machines disagree by some amount: the skew.

Operating systems expose at least two clocks. The real-time clock follows the synchronised wall time and can jump. The monotonic clock counts from an arbitrary start, never goes backwards and is not stepped by time corrections. Timeouts, rate limits and latency measurements should use the monotonic clock.

Last-write-wins resolves conflicting writes by keeping the one with the largest timestamp. When timestamps come from different machines, the order they give is only as good as the skew. A write can lose to one that really happened earlier, and nothing reports the loss.

To order updates to one item, let a single authority assign the order: the item’s owner service, a primary database that assigns a sequence or commit order, or a version column checked on every write. Clients send the version they read; a stale version is rejected instead of overwriting newer data.

When many writers must agree on what caused what, logical clocks help. A Lamport clock gives an order consistent with causality; vector clocks can also detect concurrent writes so they can be merged or shown to a user. Some databases combine bounded clock uncertainty with waiting out that bound, which needs carefully engineered time sources.

useWhen: Any service that times work, expires leases or resolves concurrent writes.
Logs and traces that must line up across machines, with skew in mind.
avoidWhen: Avoid last-write-wins on wall-clock timestamps from different machines for data that matters.
Avoid wall time for timeouts and elapsed-time checks.

numbers.title: How skew turns into lost writes
assumptions: A user saves through A, then 200 ms later through B
steps: LWW keeps A’s write because 0.300 > 0.200, so the user’s newer change is lost.
Any write on B within 300 ms after a write on A loses the same way.
numbers.result: The loss window equals the skew. Versions remove it; better synchronisation only shrinks it.

india.title: What the specifications say
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The Linux manual page for the clock functions describes a realtime clock that can be set and can jump, and a monotonic clock that cannot be set and is not affected by discontinuous jumps in system time, though it can be slewed. RFC 5905 specifies NTP version 4, which estimates the offset to time servers and disciplines the local clock, with accuracy depending on network conditions.

pitfalls.trap: “Our servers use NTP, so timestamps order events.”
pitfalls.say: “Skew is small but not zero; I’d order with versions and keep timestamps for display.”
“With the monotonic clock, so a time correction cannot break the timeout.”

takeaways: Use the monotonic clock for durations and timeouts.
Clocks on different machines disagree; state the skew you tolerate.
Last-write-wins on wall time can drop newer writes.
Order updates with versions, sequences or logical clocks.

interactive.title: Which save survives?
interactive.prompt: Server A’s clock is 300 ms fast. A user saves a draft through A, then 200 ms later saves a newer version through B. The store keeps the write with the larger timestamp. Which version is stored?

choices.label: The newer save through B
choices.feedback: B’s timestamp is 10:00:00.200, smaller than A’s 10:00:00.300, so it loses.

choices.label: The older save through A
choices.feedback: Right: A’s fast clock gives its older write the larger timestamp.

choices.label: Both, as conflicting versions
choices.feedback: Last-write-wins keeps one value; it does not report conflicts.

interactive.reveal: Last-write-wins picks the larger timestamp, not the later event. With a version number checked on each save, B’s save would be based on A’s version and both would apply in order.

seeAlso.why: Lamport and vector clocks for causal order
Idempotent endpoints that handle repeated writes
Calendar time in business rules: zones, daylight saving and local schedules

title: Load Shedding and Backpressure
objectives: Explain why a queue in front of an overloaded server makes every request late
Shed excess load early with a clear retryable reply
Use bounded queues and backpressure so producers slow down

cards.title: More work than capacity has only three outcomes
cards.body: When requests arrive faster than a server can finish them, the excess must go somewhere: it waits in a queue, it is rejected, or the sender slows down. Waiting looks kind, but past a point every request waits longer than its caller will, and the server spends all its effort on answers nobody reads.

cards.title: Worked example: 1,500 requests per second into 1,000
cards.body: A server finishes 1,000 requests per second and 1,500 arrive. Without limits, the queue grows by 500 every second: after 60 seconds it holds 30,000 requests, and a new one waits 30 seconds. With a 2-second client timeout, almost everything served is already abandoned. Rejecting the extra 500 per second keeps 1,000 good answers per second flowing.

cards.title: Shedding at the front door
cards.body: Reject early and cheaply, before work is spent.
steps: Measure in-flight requests or queue time
Above the limit, reject with 503 and a Retry-After hint
Prefer to drop low-priority work first
Bound every queue; drop requests already past their deadline
Clients back off with jitter instead of retrying at once

cards.title: Backpressure between stages
cards.body: Inside a pipeline, a full buffer should slow the stage before it rather than grow without limit. A bounded queue that blocks or refuses new items passes the pressure upstream until it reaches something that can wait, shed or scale, instead of exhausting memory in the middle.

cards.title: Trap: an unbounded queue “so nothing is lost”
cards.body: An unbounded queue turns a short overload into minutes of latency and can exhaust memory. Requests are not saved; they are delayed past usefulness. Bound the queue and decide explicitly what is rejected.

questions.prompt: Arrivals exceed capacity by 20% for ten minutes and the queue is unbounded. What happens to latency?

choices.label: It rises by about 20% and stays there
It stays flat because the queue absorbs the excess
It keeps growing for as long as the overload lasts
It falls once the server warms its caches

questions.explanation: The backlog grows every second the excess lasts, and every new request waits behind it.

questions.prompt: What reply suits a request shed because the server is overloaded?

choices.label: 400 Bad Request, as the client sent too many requests
503 Service Unavailable with a Retry-After hint
200 OK with an empty body
404 Not Found until load falls

questions.explanation: 503 says the failure is temporary and Retry-After tells well-behaved clients when to come back.

questions.prompt: Why reject at the front door rather than after partial processing?

choices.label: A late rejection gives the client a more detailed error message
Partial work is usually cached for later
Clients ignore early rejections
An early rejection is cheap; a late one wastes capacity

questions.explanation: Shedding is only useful if dropping a request is much cheaper than serving it.

questions.prompt: A parser stage feeds a slower database writer through a buffer. What prevents memory from running out?

choices.label: A bounded buffer that makes the parser wait when full
A larger in-memory buffer sized for the busiest day of the year
Writing to the database from more threads
Compressing items in the buffer

questions.explanation: Bounding the buffer pushes the slowdown upstream instead of piling items in memory.

questions.prompt: Order what a server does with a request during overload.

items.label: Reject cheaply with 503 and Retry-After if over
Process it if there is still time
Check in-flight count against the limit
Otherwise check the request’s deadline

questions.explanation: Decide cheaply first, then avoid work whose caller has already given up.

questions.prompt: 1,500 requests per second arrive at a server that finishes 1,000 per second. With an unbounded queue, how many requests are waiting after 60 seconds?
assumptions: Arrival and service rates are steady
questions.explanation: Sanity check: at 1,000 per second that backlog takes 30 s to clear, far past a 2 s timeout.

flashcards.back: Queue, reject, or slow the sender; queues alone make everyone late.
503 with Retry-After, returned before work is spent.
A full bounded buffer slows the stage before it.

mechanism.title: Why queues fail under sustained overload
steps: A server has a maximum throughput. When the arrival rate is below it, queues stay short and absorb bursts. When arrivals exceed it for long, the queue grows by the difference every second, and the waiting time for each new request grows with it. In a growing queue, a new request waits about queue length ÷ service rate. Little’s law, items equal arrival rate times time in the system, holds only once a queue is stable.

Callers have timeouts. Once the queue wait passes the timeout, the server finishes requests whose callers have gone, and it may receive retries for them on top. Throughput of useful answers falls towards zero even though the server is fully busy. This is congestion collapse.

Load shedding caps the work admitted. A server tracks in-flight requests, queue time or CPU, and above a limit rejects new requests quickly with 503 and, where sensible, Retry-After. Rejection must be far cheaper than serving, so it happens before authentication-heavy or database work where possible.

Not all requests are equal. Shedding can drop background, batch or retry traffic first and keep interactive requests. Requests already past their deadline should be dropped when dequeued. Clients must cooperate: limited retries, exponential backoff with jitter, and respect for Retry-After, or shed requests come straight back.

Backpressure is the same idea inside a system. A bounded queue between stages blocks or refuses when full, so a slow consumer slows its producer rather than letting memory grow. Pressure moves upstream until it reaches a point that can wait, shed or scale, such as the edge of the system or an autoscaler.

useWhen: Any service that can receive more traffic than it can serve, which is every public service.
Pipelines whose stages run at different speeds.
avoidWhen: Avoid unbounded queues and thread pools in request paths.
Avoid client retries without backoff, jitter and a limit.

rows: Preserved if the source can wait

numbers.title: The cost of queueing an overload
steps: Excess: 1,500 − 1,000 = 500 per second.
Queue after 60 s: 500 × 60 = 30,000 requests.
A new request waits 30,000 ÷ 1,000 = 30 s, fifteen times the timeout.
Shedding 500/s instead keeps waits near zero and 1,000 useful answers per second.
numbers.result: Shedding a third of the traffic keeps two thirds succeeding; queueing all of it lets nearly all of it fail.

india.title: What the Google SRE book recommends
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The Google SRE book’s chapter on handling overload describes servers protecting themselves by rejecting requests they cannot serve in time, client-side throttling that stops sending requests likely to be rejected, request criticality so the least important traffic is dropped first, and retry budgets that keep retries from multiplying load during an overload.

pitfalls.trap: “We queue everything so no request is lost.”
pitfalls.say: “Past the timeout the queue only delays failures; I’d bound it and shed early with 503.”
“With backoff, jitter and Retry-After, or the retries become the overload.”

takeaways: Sustained overload grows queues and latency without limit.
Shed early and cheaply with 503 and Retry-After.
Drop low-priority and expired work first.
Bound queues so backpressure reaches the source.

interactive.title: Queue it or shed it?
interactive.prompt: A server finishes 1,000 requests per second and clients time out after 2 s. Slide the arrival rate and compare a server that queues everything with one that sheds the excess, after 60 seconds.
interactive.takeaway: Even 3% over capacity, at 1,030 per second, builds a 1.8 s wait in a minute; at 1,500 the wait is 30 s and nothing useful comes out. Shedding the excess keeps up to 1,000 good answers per second however high arrivals go.

seeAlso.why: Timeouts, retries and circuit breakers that pair with shedding
Rate limiting, which caps load per client
